# Women's legal rights and suffrage (`women_rights_suffrage`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by human_equality_dignity, universal_schooling, representative_government
- Core idea: Women are full legal persons: they own and inherit property, keep their earnings, make contracts, sue, are educated like men, consent to marriage and may leave it, and vote and hold office on the same terms. Historically the order was property and schooling first, the vote last. The case that convinces is practical as well as moral: half of a people's talent is otherwise wasted, widows and wives already run farms, shops and regencies competently, and educated mothers raise healthier and better-taught children.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming women everywhere had no rights before the 19th century: Egyptian, Islamic and late Roman law let women own and manage property, while English coverture took it away on marriage
  - Starting with the vote where almost no men vote either; property rights and schooling are the reachable first steps
  - Arguing only from abstract equality: opponents cite scripture and nature, so point to existing queens, abbesses, merchants' widows and guild mistresses
  - Underrating the danger: Olympe de Gouges was guillotined in 1793, and a woman who speaks in public can be charged with scolding or witchcraft
- History: egypt: from c. 2500 BC – women own, inherit and bequeath property, make contracts and sue in their own names; mesopotamia: c. 1754 BC – Hammurabi protects dowries and lets certain priestesses (naditu) trade and own property independently; india: early Buddhist order of nuns (c. 5th–4th c. BC); dharma texts recognise women's own property (stridhana); 1950 universal adult suffrage; china: Song law (10th–13th c.) gives daughters dowry and some inheritance shares; property rights narrow under the Ming; 1947–1949 equal suffrage; islamic: 7th c. – a wife keeps her own property and dower and can contract; inheritance shares depend on kinship (a daughter sharing with a son receives half his share); women founded many endowments; 1930–1934 Turkey grants the vote; americas: Haudenosaunee clan mothers choose and can depose chiefs; 1776–1807 New Jersey lets propertied women vote; 1848 Seneca Falls declaration; 1869 Wyoming Territory; europe: 1405 – Christine de Pizan, The Book of the City of Ladies; 1791 Olympe de Gouges; 1792 Wollstonecraft; 1870–1882 British Married Women's Property Acts; 1906 Finland grants women equal rights to vote and stand for parliament; women elected in 1907; 1971 Switzerland; global: 1893 – New Zealand, first self-governing country where all women vote in national elections
- Read:
  - Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792)
  - John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women (1869)
  - Christine de Pizan, The Book of the City of Ladies (1405)
